name: Mongolia Buriat
confidence_why: The rule comes from Walker's 1997 unpublished manuscript, whose Buriat consultant data name no dialect or country and are only said to agree with Poppe's 1960 grammar of literary Buriat, while Badagarov 2017, drawing on Budaev's 1981 instrumental study of Khori Buriat, describes a fixed final pitch accent that long vowels do not attract and notes that Buriat dialects differ in stress, so nothing read supports a weight-sensitive rule for the Buriat of Mongolia.

catalog_quote: Another East Mongolian language, Buriat, provides a second example of a rightmost heavy else leftmost pattern with quantity-sensitive nonfinality. The following data are from the same study as that outlined for Khalkha. Findings are consistent with the description of Buriat given by Poppe (1960: 19) and again clarify the interpretation of 'penultimate' heavy syllable. Like Khalkha, primary stress falls on the last syllable if it is the only heavy in the word, otherwise on the rightmost nonfinal heavy, otherwise on the initial syllable. Secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and (possibly) the initial syllable when they do not receive primary stress. (33) Buriat: Lè L [xáda] 'mountain'; Lò Hè [xàdáar] 'through the mountain'; Hê Hò [bóosòo] 'bet, wager'; Lò Hè Hò [dàláigàar] 'by sea' ... tone_statements.citation: Budaev, Bal'zhinima Zhambalovich. 1984. Aktsentuatsiya buryatskogo yazyka (opyt eksperimental'no-foneticheskogo issledovaniya slovesnogo i sintagmaticheskogo udareniya) [Accentuation of Buryat: an experimental-phonetic study of word and syntagmatic stress]. Dissertatsiya.. kandidata filologicheskikh nauk, spetsial'nost' VAK 10.02.16 (Mongol'skie yazyki). 185 pp. (research done at LEFI IIFF SO AN SSSR, Novosibirsk, under V. M. Nadelyaev).
tone_statements.quote: Словесное ударение, относящееся к слову как базовой единице немоносиллабического нетонального языка, каким является бурятский язык, в высказывании подвергается влиянию вцутри-фразовой организации значимых единиц различной протяженности, будь то синтагма или фраза. [...] Итак, в бурятском языке имеется словесное и синтагматическое ударение. Словесное ударение конституируется повышением основного тона на конечном слоге изолированной словоформы.
tone_statements.translation: Word stress, which belongs to the word as the basic unit of a non-monosyllabic, non-tonal language such as Buryat, is subject within the utterance to the influence of the intra-phrasal organisation of meaningful units of various extent, be it the syntagma or the phrase. [...] Thus, Buryat has word stress and syntagmatic stress. Word stress is constituted by a rise of the fundamental tone on the final syllable of the isolated word form.
tone_statements.locator: disserCat record: 'Vvedenie dissertatsii (chast' avtoreferata)' (theoretical premises paragraph) and the closing summary ('Itak, v buryatskom yazyke..') of the displayed text; dissertation ch. IV 'Tonal'nost'' pp. 108-136 per its table of contents
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone (language explicitly 'netonal'nyi'); word prominence = obligatory F0 rise on the word-final syllable (F0 low on the first syllable), length-independent, with syntagma-initial phrasal stress superimposed in connected speech (Khori dialect, instrumental).

audit.recode_to: Fold into russ1264 (or parent buri1258) as one 'Buriat (Walker 1997)' record, or mark mong1330 as inherited-from-generic-Buriat with a caution; then re-read the surviving record against Budaev 1981 / Poppe 1960 p. 19 before keeping classification weight.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check passes: the deciding passage and every cited Buriat form are in the held Walker June 1997 ms. text (lines 1431-1447, pp. 26-27, ex. 33) and the ROA-172 cross-check (56)-(57) is on p. 24 = printed p. 27. (2) The deciding source is a 1996/97 unpublished OT typology ms; its methods footnote documents only a Khalkha speaker from Ulaanbaatar, the Buriat forms are 'from the same study' with no speaker/dialect/country given, and the benchmark is Poppe 1960 (literary Buriat, Russia). Nothing links the data to Mongolia Buriat, and the catalog's russ1264 'Buriat' record is coded from the identical passage, so mong1330 is a duplicate entity by our rule that each source is filed under the language's current Glottolog code (a retired code does not make a separate language) rather than an independent description. (3) Independent primaries disagree with the weight-driven coding: Poppe 1938 sec. 53 pp. 62-63 (held under our earlier reading, opened) gives initial expiratory stress

sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Distinguishes a Khalkha type (first long vowel/diphthong attracts the pitch accent; with only short vowels the last closed syllable) from a 'Buryat-Oirat type' with constant final-syllable musical (tonal) stress in which long vowels do NOT attract the pitch rise and are pronounced extra-long when unstressed (bur. xaagaa -> [xaaa'gaa]); cites Budaev 1981 (instrumental, Khori dialect) for final tonal stress; notes Khori Buryat patterns with Kalmyk while Zakamensk Buryat stress/intonation is 'close to the Khalkha type'.
sources.locator: pp. 113-115 (raw the text); reference list cites Budaev 1981: 97, 104, 108
sources.note: Open survey by a Buryat phonologist classing Buryat (Khori) as final pitch-rise, length-insensitive, and noting southern (Zakamensk) Buryat is Khalkha-like; directly relevant to whether a Mongolia-Buriat record should carry the Khalkha-type weight rule

sources.note: Instrumental (pneumo-oscillographic + spectrographic) test of four candidate correlates of Buryat word stress - quantity, intensity, tenseness/timbre, tonality (F0) - with a whole chapter IV 'Tonal'nost''. Conclusion read online: Buryat is explicitly called a non-tonal polysyllabic language; word stress is constituted by an obligatory F0 rise on the final syllable of the isolated word form (F0 minimum on the first syllable, interval from a second to a fifth), intensity inconsistent/neutralised, tenseness irrelevant for Khori; in connected speech a syntagma-initial syntagmatic stress overlays…
